refsect1.title: Description
refsect1.para: udev supplies the system software with device events, manages permissions of device nodes, may create additional symlinks in the /dev directory and may rename network interfaces. The kernel usually just assigns unpredictable device names based on the order of discovery. Meaningful symlinks or network device names provide a way to reliably identify devices based on their properties or current configuration.

The udev daemon, udevd 8, receives device uevents directly from the kernel whenever a device is added or removed from the system, or it changes its state. When udev receives a device event, it matches its configured set of rules against various device attributes to identify the device. Rules that match may provide additional device information to be stored in the udev database or to be used to create meaningful symlink names.
All device information udev processes is stored in the udev database and sent out to possible event subscribers. Access to all stored data and the event sources is provided by the library libudev.

refsect1.title: Rules Files
refsect1.para: The udev rules are read from the files located in the system rules directories /lib/udev/rules.d (additionally /usr/lib/udev/rules.d when built with --enable-split-usr) and /usr/local/lib/udev/rules.d, the volatile runtime directory /run/udev/rules.d and the local administration directory /etc/udev/rules.d. All rules files are collectively sorted and processed in lexical order, regardless of the directories in which they live. However, files with identical filenames replace each other. Files in /etc have the highest priority, files in /run take precedence over files with the same name in /usr/local/lib, and these over files with the same name in /lib (or /usr/lib). This can be used to override a system-supplied rules file with a local file if needed; a symlink in /etc with the same name as a rules file in /lib, pointing to /dev/null, disables the rules file entirely. Rule files must have the extension .rules; other extensions are ignored.

Every line in the rules file contains at least one key-value pair. Except for empty lines or lines beginning with #, which are ignored. There are two kinds of keys: match and assignment. If all match keys match against their values, the rule gets applied and the assignment keys get the specified values assigned.
A matching rule may rename a network interface, add symlinks pointing to the device node, or run a specified program as part of the event handling.

A rule consists of a comma-separated list of one or more key-value pairs. Each key has a distinct operation, depending on the used operator. A rule line with a key-value pair that cannot be parsed, e.g. with a value that is not quoted, or with an unknown key, an operator the key does not take, an unknown built-in command, or an unknown type of IMPORT{} or RUN{}, is ignored as a whole, and an error message says so. Valid operators are:

listitem.para: Compare for equality.
Compare for inequality.
Assign a value to a key. Keys that represent a list are reset and only this single value is assigned.
Add the value to a key that holds a list of entries.
Remove the value from a key that holds a list of entries.
Assign a value to a key finally; disallow any later changes.

refsect1.para: Values are written as double quoted strings, such as ("string"). To include a quotation mark (") in the value, precede it by a backslash (\"). Any other occurrences of a backslash followed by a character are not unescaped. That is, "\t\n" is treated as four characters: backslash, lowercase t, backslash, lowercase n.

The string can be prefixed with a lowercase e (e"string\n") to mark the string as C-style escaped, see Escape sequences in C. For example, e"string\n" is parsed as 7 characters: 6 lowercase letters and a newline. This can be useful for writing special characters when a kernel driver requires them.

The string can be prefixed with a lowercase i (i"string") to mark that the string or pattern will match case-insensitively. For example, i"foo" will match foo, FOO, FoO and so on. The prefix can be used only for match (==) or unmatch (!=) rules, e.g. ATTR{foo}==i"abcd".
Please note that NUL is not allowed in either string variant.

Rules written for systemd-udevd may use features which udev does not provide: the CONST{arch}, CONST{virt} and CONST{cvm} match keys, and the dissect_image, net_setup_link and uaccess built-in commands. A rule line using one of them is ignored as a whole, with an error message saying so.

The following key names can be used to match against device properties. Some of the keys also match against properties of the parent devices in sysfs, not only the device that has generated the event. If multiple keys that match a parent device are specified in a single rule, all these keys must match at one and the same parent device.

listitem.para: Match the name of the event action.
Match the devpath of the event device.
Match the name of the event device.
Match the name of a network interface. It can be used once the NAME key has been set in one of the preceding rules.

Match the name of a symlink targeting the node. It can be used once a SYMLINK key has been set in one of the preceding rules. There may be multiple symlinks; only one needs to match. If the operator is !=, the token returns true only if there is no symlink matched.
Match the subsystem of the event device.
Match the driver name of the event device. Only set this key for devices which are bound to a driver at the time the event is generated.
Match sysfs attribute values of the event device. Trailing whitespace in the attribute values is ignored unless the specified match value itself contains trailing whitespace.
Match a kernel parameter value.
Search the devpath upwards for a matching device name.
Search the devpath upwards for a matching device subsystem name.
Search the devpath upwards for a matching device driver name.

Search the devpath upwards for a device with matching sysfs attribute values. If multiple ATTRS matches are specified, all of them must match on the same device. Trailing whitespace in the attribute values is ignored unless the specified match value itself contains trailing whitespace.
Match against a device property value. When the device does not have the property, the global property set with udevadm control --property is matched, if there is one.

Match against one of device tags. It can be used once a TAG key has been set in one of the preceding rules. There may be multiple tags; only one needs to match. If the operator is !=, the token returns true only if there is no tag matched. Only the current tags, those assigned while processing this event, are matched, not the tags which remain from earlier events.
Test the existence of a file. An octal mode mask can be specified if needed.

Execute a program to determine whether there is a match; the key is true if the program returns successfully. The device properties are made available to the executed program in the environment. The program's standard output is available in the RESULT key.
This can only be used for very short-running foreground tasks. For details, see RUN.
Match the returned string of the last PROGRAM call. This key can be used in the same or in any later rule after a PROGRAM call.

refsect1.para: Most of the fields support shell glob pattern matching and alternate patterns. The following special characters are supported:

listitem.para: Matches zero or more characters.
Matches any single character.

Matches any single character specified within the brackets. For example, the pattern string tty[SR] would match either ttyS or ttyR. Ranges are also supported via the - character. For example, to match on the range of all digits, the pattern [0-9] could be used. If the first character following the [ is a !, any characters not enclosed are matched.
Separates alternative patterns. For example, the pattern string abc|x* would match either abc or x*.

refsect1.para: The following keys can get values assigned:

listitem.para: The name to use for a network interface. The name of a device node cannot be changed by udev, only additional symlinks can be created.

As in systemd, a network interface name is valid if it has 1 to 15 printable ASCII characters other than space, :, / and %, is not only digits, and is not ., .., all or default. With the naming schemes v249 and later (see ), all other characters are replaced by _, and a name that is still not valid is ignored with a warning. With the older schemes, only the characters that are not allowed in symlink names (see SYMLINK) are replaced, and renaming the interface to an invalid name fails. No characters are replaced with OPTIONS+="string_escape=none".

The name of a symlink targeting the node. Every matching rule adds this value to the list of symlinks to be created. With the -= operator, the specified symlinks are removed from that list again, which allows suppressing symlinks added by earlier rules.

The set of characters to name a symlink is limited. Allowed characters are 0-9A-Za-z#+-.:=@_/, valid UTF-8 character sequences, and \x00 hex encoding. All other characters are replaced by a _ character.

The name is taken relative to /dev/, and may also be given as an absolute path below /dev/. It is normalized: redundant slashes, . components and trailing slashes are removed, e.g. disk//by-foo/./bar/ results in /dev/disk/by-foo/bar. A name with a .. component or with a component longer than 255 bytes, a name with control characters, which are only kept with OPTIONS+="string_escape=none", an absolute path outside of /dev/, and a name that refers to /dev/ itself are refused with an error message. The symlinks recorded in the udev database of a device are normalized and checked in the same way. A symlink is not created, and a warning is logged, where a file or directory that is not a symlink exists.

Multiple symlinks may be specified by separating the names by the space character. In case multiple devices claim the same name, the link always points to the device with the highest link_priority. If the current device goes away, the links are re-evaluated and the device with the next highest link_priority becomes the owner of the link. If no link_priority is specified, the order of the devices (and which one of them owns the link) is undefined.
Symlink names must never conflict with the kernel's default device node names, as that would result in unpredictable behavior.
The permissions for the device node. Every specified value overrides the compiled-in default value.
Applies the specified Linux Security Module label to the device node.
The value that should be written to a sysfs attribute of the event device.
The value that should be written to kernel parameter.

Set a device property value. Property names with a leading . are not stored in the database. Like all other properties, they are passed in the environment of the programs run by RUN, PROGRAM and IMPORT{program}, and are sent with the event to the event listeners.

A property name may only contain ASCII letters, digits, _ and ., and a value must be valid UTF-8 without control characters, like newlines or tabs. Other properties are refused: an assignment or an IMPORT logs a warning and the rest of the rule is still applied, and invalid properties set by built-in commands or received with the kernel event are ignored. Assigning an empty value, also as the result of substitutions, removes the property.

The properties that udev sets itself cannot be assigned: ACTION, SEQNUM, SYNTH_UUID, DEVPATH, DEVPATH_OLD, SUBSYSTEM, DEVTYPE, DRIVER, MODALIAS, DEVNAME, DEVMODE, DEVUID, DEVGID, MAJOR, MINOR, DISKSEQ, PARTN, IFINDEX, INTERFACE, INTERFACE_OLD, DEVLINKS, TAGS, CURRENT_TAGS, USEC_INITIALIZED, UDEV_DATABASE_VERSION, and names starting with SYNTH_ARG_. A rule line assigning one of them is invalid, and is ignored as a whole.

Attach a tag to a device. This is used to filter events for users of libudev's monitor functionality, or to enumerate a group of tagged devices. The implementation can only work efficiently if only a few tags are attached to a device. It is only meant to be used in contexts with specific device filter requirements, and not as a general-purpose flag. Excessive use might result in inefficient event handling.

Tags are "sticky": a tag attached by one event stays attached to the device, in the TAGS property and in the index of tagged devices, until the device is removed, so that programs filtering events by tag also see the events of the device after the tag is no longer assigned. The tags assigned while processing the most recent event are the current tags, in the CURRENT_TAGS property.

A tag name may only contain ASCII letters, digits, - and _; other names are ignored with an error. += attaches the tag. -= removes it from the current tags only. = and := first clear the current tags, and drop the tags attached earlier while processing this event, and then attach the tag; TAG="" only clears them.
Add a program to the list of programs to be executed after processing all the rules for a specific event, depending on type:
Execute an external program specified as the assigned value. If no absolute path is given, the program is expected to live in /lib/udev, otherwise, the absolute path must be specified.
This is the default if no type is specified.
As program, but use one of the built-in programs rather than an external one.

The program name and following arguments are separated by spaces. Single quotes can be used to specify arguments with spaces. The name of a builtin and its arguments are separated by any whitespace; single and double quotes, also in the middle of an argument, group characters including whitespace and are removed.
This can only be used for very short-running foreground tasks. Running an event process for a long period of time may block all further events for this or a dependent device.
Starting daemons or other long-running processes is not appropriate for udev; the forked processes, detached or not, will be unconditionally killed after the event handling has finished.
A named label to which a GOTO may jump.
Jumps to the next LABEL with a matching name.
Import a set of variables as device properties, depending on type:

Execute an external program specified as the assigned value and import its output, which must be in environment key format. Path specification, command/argument separation, and quoting work like in RUN.
Similar to program, but use one of the built-in programs rather than an external one.

Import a text file specified as the assigned value, the content of which must be in environment key format. A line may be up to 1 MiB long; a longer line stops the import, and the key is false, while the properties imported before it are kept.
Import a single property specified as the assigned value from the current device database. This works only if the database is already populated by an earlier event.

Import a single property from the kernel command line. For simple flags the value of the property is set to 1. Options starting with rd. are only imported in an initrd, see udevd8; the prefix is part of the key, i.e. IMPORT{cmdline}="foo" does not import rd.foo. For testing, the kernel command line can be replaced with the $UDEV_PROC_CMDLINE environment variable, see udevd8.

Import the stored keys from the parent device by reading the database entry of the parent device. The value assigned to IMPORT{parent} is used as a filter of key names to import (with the same shell glob pattern matching used for comparisons). The import is successful when at least one property was imported.
This can only be used for very short-running foreground tasks. For details see RUN.

Note that multiple IMPORT{} keys may be specified in one rule, and =, :=, and += have the same effect as ==. The key is true if the import is successful, unless != is used as the operator which causes the key to be true if the import failed.

Rule and device options. Several options may be given in one value, separated by commas, e.g. OPTIONS+="watch,link_priority=10"; each one must be exactly one of the options below. An unknown option is ignored with a warning, and the rest of the rule is applied. An invalid value of link_priority= or log_level= makes the rule line invalid, as do the operators ==, != and -=; += has the same effect as =.
Specify the priority of the created symlinks. Devices with higher priorities overwrite existing symlinks of other devices. The default is 0.

When replace, possibly unsafe characters in strings assigned to NAME, SYMLINK, and ENV{key} are replaced. When none, no replacement is performed. When unset, the replacement is performed for NAME, SYMLINK, but not for ENV{key}. Defaults to unset.

Apply the permissions specified in this rule to the static device node with the specified name. Static device node creation can be requested by kernel modules. These nodes might not have a corresponding kernel device at the time udevd is started; they can trigger automatic kernel module loading.

Assign alternative names to a network interface when it is added. After the add event is processed and the interface is renamed, if requested, the values of the ID_NET_NAME_FROM_DATABASE, ID_NET_NAME_ONBOARD, ID_NET_NAME_SLOT, ID_NET_NAME_PATH and ID_NET_NAME_MAC properties that are valid alternative names, i.e. valid interface names (see NAME) with up to 127 characters, and differ from the name of the interface, are assigned to it as alternative names, like the default AlternativeNamesPolicy= of systemd does. Names that the interface already has are not assigned again, names used by other interfaces are skipped. As in systemd, they are not assigned when renaming the interface fails, unless it is up. Alternative names require Linux 5.5 or later, older kernels are silently ignored. udevadm test does not assign them, but shows them, like systemd, also the name the interface would get. Nothing is done when net_altnames=no is set in udev.conf5.
Watch the device node with inotify; when the node is closed after being opened for writing, a change uevent is synthesized.
Disable the watching of a device node with inotify.

Set the flag (sticky bit) on the udev database entry of the event device. Device properties are then kept in the database even when udevadm info --cleanup-db is called. This option can be useful in certain cases (e.g. Device Mapper devices) for persisting device state on the transition from initramfs.

Takes a log level name like debug or info, or a special value reset. When a log level name is specified, the maximum log level is changed to that level. When reset is set, then the previously specified log level is revoked. Defaults to the log level of the main process of udevd.

This may be useful when debugging events for certain devices. Note that the log level is applied when the line including this rule is processed. So, for debugging, it is recommended that this is specified at earlier place, e.g., the first line of 00-debug.rules.
Example for debugging uevent processing for network interfaces. # /etc/udev/rules.d/00-debug-net.rules SUBSYSTEM=="net", OPTIONS="log_level=debug"
Dump the status of the event currently processing. It may be useful for debugging udev rules by inserting this option.
Similar to dump, but dump the status of the event in JSON format.

refsect1.para: The NAME, SYMLINK, PROGRAM, OWNER, GROUP, MODE, SECLABEL, and RUN fields support simple string substitutions. The substitutions are performed while the individual rule is being processed, so they use the device properties set by the preceding rules. The available substitutions are:

listitem.para: The kernel name for this device.
The kernel number for this device. For example, sda3 has kernel number 3.
The devpath of the device.
The name of the device matched while searching the devpath upwards for SUBSYSTEMS, KERNELS, DRIVERS, and ATTRS.
The driver name of the device matched while searching the devpath upwards for SUBSYSTEMS, KERNELS, DRIVERS, and ATTRS.

The value of a sysfs attribute found at the device where all keys of the rule have matched. If the matching device does not have such an attribute, and a previous KERNELS, SUBSYSTEMS, DRIVERS, or ATTRS test selected a parent device, then the attribute from that parent device is used.
If the attribute is a symlink, the last element of the symlink target is returned as the value.
A device property value. When the device does not have the property, the value of the global property set with udevadm control --property, if there is one.
The kernel major number for the device.
The kernel minor number for the device.

The string returned by the external program requested with PROGRAM. A single part of the string, separated by a space character, may be selected by specifying the part number as an attribute: %c{N}. If the number is followed by the + character, this part plus all remaining parts of the result string are substituted: %c{N+}.
The node name of the parent device.
The current name of the device. If not changed by a rule, it is the name of the kernel device.
A space-separated list of the current symlinks. The value is only set during a remove event or if an earlier rule assigned a value.
The sysfs mount point.
The name of the device node.
The % character itself.
The $ character itself.

refsect1.title: Built-in Commands
refsect1.para: Built-in commands are run with IMPORT{builtin} and RUN{builtin}. udevadm test-builtin --help lists the available builtins, and udevadm test-builtin runs one on a device and prints the properties it sets. The builtins and properties described here are compatible with systemd-udevd.

refsect2.title: blkid
refsect2.para: blkid [--offset=bytes] [--hint=name=value] [--noraid] probes a block device for file systems and partition tables with libblkid and sets ID_FS_* and ID_PART_* properties. Among them:

listitem.para: The volume, logical volume, volume set and data preparer identifiers, which libblkid 2.37 and newer reports for e.g. ISO 9660 and UDF file systems. Like in ID_FS_LABEL_ENC=, characters that are not safe are encoded as \xnn.

Set on the whole disk with a GPT partition table that the root file system is expected on, together with the partition UUID of its root partition, if it has one. In the initrd, this is the disk that carries the EFI System Partition or the XBOOTLDR partition whose partition UUID the boot loader reports in the LoaderDevicePartUUID-4a67b082-0a4c-41cf-b6c7-440b29bb8c4f EFI variable (systemd-boot and GRUB with the bli module set it), or, without that variable, a loop device whose backing file name is rootdisk or rootdisk.raw. The root partition is the partition with the root partition type of the native architecture (e.g. 4f68bce3-e8cd-4db1-96e7-fbcaf984b709 on x86-64) that has the newest version in its label; partitions with the no-auto flag (bit 63) and partitions labelled _empty are skipped. After the initrd, it is the disk that the root file system is on (also through dm-crypt, dm-verity or a single-device btrfs), and the partition that holds it, if it has the root partition type. The initrd is recognized by /etc/initrd-release and a tmpfs or ramfs root file system. Only whole disks with partition scanning enabled are considered.

Set on the partition whose partition UUID matches ID_PART_GPT_AUTO_ROOT_UUID= of its disk. 90-image-dissect.rules creates the symlink /dev/gpt-auto-root for it, or /dev/gpt-auto-root-luks if it is a LUKS volume. While a factory reset is in progress (ID_FACTORY_RESET=on, see below), it gets /dev/gpt-auto-root-ignore-factory-reset or /dev/gpt-auto-root-luks-ignore-factory-reset instead, and once the factory reset is complete, both. When the LUKS volume is unlocked as a device mapper device named root, that device gets /dev/gpt-auto-root, and also /dev/gpt-auto-root-ignore-factory-reset while a factory reset is in progress or complete.

refsect2.title: factory_reset
refsect2.para: factory_reset status sets ID_FACTORY_RESET= to the factory reset state, as systemd determines it, so that rules can e.g. ignore devices while a factory reset is in progress:

listitem.para: The environment variable $SYSTEMD_FACTORY_RESET_SUPPORTED of the udev daemon is set to false.
/run/systemd/factory-reset-complete exists.

The kernel command line option systemd.factory_reset= (or systemd.factory-reset=) is set to true or false; the option without a value means true. If it is not set, the state is on if the FactoryResetRequest-8cf2644b-4b0b-428f-9387-6d876050dc67 EFI variable requests a factory reset for this boot: it holds a JSON object whose osReleaseId and osReleaseImageId members match ID= and IMAGE_ID= of /etc/os-release (or /usr/lib/os-release, or the file that $SYSTEMD_OS_RELEASE names), and whose bootId member differs from the current boot ID (/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id).
The EFI variable requests a factory reset for the next boot: its bootId is the current boot ID.
None of the above: the system was not booted with EFI, or the EFI variable is not set, not valid, or meant for another operating system.

refsect2.para: The checks are done in the order listed. If the state cannot be determined, e.g. because systemd.factory_reset= has a value that is not a boolean or os-release cannot be read, the property is not set.

refsect2.title: tpm2_id
refsect2.para: tpm2_id identify, which 60-tpm2-id.rules runs on /dev/tpmrmN, identifies TPM 2.0 chips. Like systemd, it starts up the TPM if the firmware has not done so, and only identifies TPMs that support AES-128 in CFB mode, which systemd requires for session encryption; other TPMs are skipped without an error. It talks to the TPM through the kernel's device node and needs no TPM libraries. It sets:

listitem.para: The manufacturer code and the vendor string that the TPM reports, with whitespace, control characters and non-ASCII bytes replaced by _.

A string that describes the TPM for hwdb lookups. It lists the family indicator (fi), level (lv), revision (rv), year (sy) and day of year (sd) of the specification, the manufacturer (mf), the vendor string (vs), the vendor TPM type in hexadecimal (ty) and the firmware version (fw), each after its two letter code and followed by a colon, e.g. fi2.0:lv0:rv1.16:sy2019:sd346:mfSTM:vsST33HTPHAHD8:ty1:fw73.4.65536:. 60-tpm2-id.rules looks up tpm2: followed by it in the hwdb; 60-tpm2.hwdb sets TPM2_BROKEN_NVPCR=1 on TPMs on which the NV index based PCRs of systemd do not work.

refsect2.para: This builtin and 60-tpm2-id.rules are left out when eudev is configured with --disable-tpm2; a rule line that uses the builtin is then ignored with an error message saying so.

refsect1.title: Network Interface Naming
refsect1.para: For network interfaces, the net_id builtin, which is imported by 75-net-description.rules, generates predictable names from firmware information, from the location of the device on its bus, and from its MAC address, and exports them as device properties. Depending on the net.ifnames= kernel command line option (see udevd 8), 80-net-name-slot.rules renames the interface to the first one of ID_NET_NAME_FROM_DATABASE, ID_NET_NAME_ONBOARD, ID_NET_NAME_SLOT, ID_NET_NAME_PATH and ID_NET_NAME_MAC that is a valid interface name (see NAME), e.g. not longer than 15 characters, as systemd does, unless an earlier rule assigned NAME=. This is the order of the default NamePolicy= of systemd, which however does not use ID_NET_NAME_MAC. Like its keep and kernel policies, the interface is not renamed when its name was given by userspace, i.e. when it was created with a name or was already renamed, or when the kernel says it named it predictably, i.e. when the name_assign_type attribute of the interface is 3 (NET_NAME_USER), 4 (NET_NAME_RENAMED) or 2 (NET_NAME_PREDICTABLE). ID_NET_NAME_FROM_DATABASE is not set by net_id, but by the hwdb, e.g. to idrac for the virtual USB network interface of Dell iDRAC by 20-net-ifname.hwdb, which 75-net-description.rules imports for USB and PCI devices.

80-net-altnames.rules requests OPTIONS+="net_altnames", so that these names, except the one the interface is renamed to, are also assigned as alternative names of the interface, also the ones longer than 15 characters, like systemd does by default. That is independent of net.ifnames=, and it is also done for interfaces that are not renamed, and with the rule generator, which replaces 80-net-name-slot.rules. The alternative names are shown by e.g. ip link show, and can be used instead of the interface name by ip and other tools. This can be disabled with net_altnames=no in udev.conf5.

All names start with a two character prefix for the type of the interface: en for Ethernet, ib for InfiniBand, sl for serial line IP (slip), wl for wireless LAN, ww for wireless WAN and mc for MCTP. Names that do not fit into the 15 characters of an interface name are exported as well, up to 127 characters, but 80-net-name-slot.rules does not rename the interface to them. The following properties are set:

listitem.para: The naming scheme the names were generated with, see below.
The index number the firmware provides for an on-board PCI device (ACPI _DSM or SMBIOS type 41), or the index of the DeviceTree alias (ethernetN, wifiN) of the device.
The label the firmware provides for an on-board PCI device. It is not used as an interface name.
The PCI slot number of the device, as provided by the firmware; the IBM PowerVM VIO slot number; the Xen netfront VIF number.

The location of the device: the PCI bus, slot and function numbers; the bus ID of an s390 CCW device, without leading zeros; the ACPI name of an ARM64 platform device; the address and port name of a netdevsim device; the port chain of a USB device on a USB host controller that is not a PCI device.

The permanent MAC address of the device. As in systemd since version 250, it is also set for an address of all zeros, except in the eudev scheme, but such a name, e.g. enx000000000000, is not unique, and 80-net-name-slot.rules never renames an interface to it.

refsect1.para: The parts of the PCI based names are:

listitem.para: The PCI domain, only when it is not 0, or as the ID_NET_NAME_INCLUDE_DOMAIN= property of the PCI device says. It is left out of slot names when the slot of an s390 PCI device is found by its function_id.
The PCI function; for multi-function devices also for function 0. With ARI, the full 8-bit function number.
The port name or, when there is none, the port number of one of several ports of a single PCI function.
An SR-IOV virtual function representor, named after the physical function, with the number of the virtual function instead of the port.
An SR-IOV virtual function, named after its physical function.
An auxiliary sub-function (e.g. of mlx5_core), named after its PCI function.
A USB device: the chain of hub port numbers, the configuration unless it is 1 and the interface unless it is 0.
A Broadcom bus (BCMA) core, unless it is 0.

refsect2.title: Naming schemes
refsect2.para: New versions add new kinds of names and improve existing ones, which changes the names of some devices. The naming logic of the net_id builtin of a given version is called a naming scheme, and it can be selected with net_naming_scheme= in udev.conf5 or net.naming_scheme= on the kernel command line (see udevd8), which takes precedence, to keep the names stable. The environment variable $NET_NAMING_SCHEME may also be used, e.g. to preview the names with udevadm test-builtin net_id; it takes precedence over both, unless it is prefixed with :. The schemes v238 and later are the ones of systemd and generate the same names as systemd does. The default is latest. Unknown names are ignored with a warning, and the next setting in the order above is used.

A naming scheme selects only the names that net_id generates, i.e. the ID_NET_NAME_* properties. Which one of them an interface is renamed to is decided by 80-net-name-slot.rules as described above, the same way with all schemes, e.g. ID_NET_NAME_FROM_DATABASE is preferred, and interfaces named by userspace or predictably by the kernel are not renamed, also with the eudev scheme, which eudev 3.2.15 did not do. The following schemes are defined:

listitem.para: The names generated by the net_id builtin of eudev 3.2.15 and older, which are based on those of systemd 220.

The naming of systemd 238. Compared to eudev: virtio network devices are named after their PCI or CCW device; onboard indexes above 16383 are ignored; the port name (nphys_port_name) is preferred over the port number; the names of s390 CCW devices are encbus_id without leading zeros, instead of enccwbus_id; IBM PowerVM VIO and ARM64 ACPI platform devices are named; the hotplug slot of a parent PCI device is used when the device has none, and slot names with leading zeros, like those of s390, are parsed as octal numbers; ID_NET_LABEL_ONBOARD is also set for devices without an onboard index; and the ID_NET_NAME_ALLOW and ID_NET_NAME_INCLUDE_DOMAIN properties are used.
SR-IOV virtual functions are named after their physical function with a vnumber suffix. Devices using ARI (e.g. NPAR partitions) use the full function number.
InfiniBand devices get names with the ib prefix. An onboard index of 0 is used.
Same names as v240.
netdevsim devices are named. ID_NET_LABEL_ONBOARD is not prefixed with the interface type anymore.
Same names as v243.
ID_NET_NAME_SLOT is not set when the slot belongs to a PCI bridge, as all devices behind it would get the same name.
The slots of s390 PCI devices are found by their function_id. Onboard indexes up to 65535 are used.
Xen netfront devices are named.
The slot of a PCI bridge is used again for multi-function devices behind it. This is reverted in v255.
Devices with a DeviceTree ethernetN alias are named.
USB devices on a USB host controller that is not a PCI device are named.
SR-IOV virtual function representors are named with an rnumber suffix instead of their port name.
The change of v251 is reverted.
The PCI slot is read from firmware_node/sun. The DeviceTree alias of the network interface itself is preferred over the one of its parent device.
Same names as v257.
WLAN devices with a DeviceTree wifiN or ethernetN alias are named.
MCTP devices are named, with the mc prefix.
Auxiliary sub-functions are named after their PCI function with an Ssfnum suffix.
The latest scheme, currently v261.

refsect2.para: Note that a naming scheme only fixes the rules; the names may still change when a new kernel version exposes more information, e.g. a phys_port_name attribute.

refsect2.title: Limiting the use of sysfs attributes
refsect2.para: With the systemd naming schemes, the sysfs attributes used for a name can be restricted with properties of the device the attribute belongs to. ID_NET_NAME_ALLOW=0 disallows all attributes that are not explicitly allowed, and ID_NET_NAME_ALLOW_ATTRIBUTE= allows (1) or disallows (0) a specific attribute, e.g. ID_NET_NAME_ALLOW_PHYS_PORT_NAME=0. For network interfaces, such properties are usually set in the hwdb, where 75-net-description.rules looks them up with the key net:naming:drdriver:, for example:

refsect1.title: Hardware Database Files
refsect1.para: The hwdb files are read from the files located in the system hwdb directory /usr/lib/udev/hwdb.d, the local administration directory /etc/udev/hwdb.d, and any other directory in the UDEV_HWDB_PATH search path variable. All hwdb files are collectively sorted and processed in lexical order, regardless of the directories in which they live. However, files with identical filenames replace each other. Files in /etc have the highest priority, then files in /usr/lib, and the ones in UDEV_HWDB_PATH comes last. Files with higher priority take precedence over files with the same name and lower priority. This order can be used to override a system-supplied hwdb file with a local file if needed; a symlink in /etc with the same name as a hwdb file in /usr/lib or UDEV_HWDB_PATH, pointing to /dev/null, disables the hwdb file entirely. hwdb files must have the extension .hwdb; other extensions are ignored.

The hwdb file contains data records consisting of matches and associated key-value pairs. Every record in the hwdb starts with one or more match string, specifying a shell glob to compare the database lookup string against. Multiple match lines are specified in additional consecutive lines. Every match line is compared individually, they are combined by OR. Every match line must start at the first character of the line.

The match lines are followed by one or more key-value pair lines, which are recognized by a leading space character. The key name and value are separated by =. An empty line signifies the end of a record. Lines beginning with # are ignored.

The content of all hwdb files is read by udevadm8 and compiled to a binary database located at /etc/udev/hwdb.bin, or alternatively /usr/lib/udev/hwdb.bin, if you want to ship the compiled database in an immutable image by using --usr, or anywhere on the system by using --output. If UDEV_HWDB_BIN is set at run-time, and its value identifies a file in the file system, then the binary database located under this name will be used. During runtime only the binary database is used.
